title: How do we find 116 × 5 and 824 × 25 quickly?
description: Ruhee finds one hundred sixteen times five by multiplying by ten and halving, and Laksh finds eight hundred twenty four times twenty five by multiplying by one hundred and dividing by four. Keeko then raises a hand, thinking multiplying by ten already gives the answer.
teaching_notes: One idea: multiply by five as times ten then halve, and by twenty five as times a hundred then divide by four. Ask the class why the first step gives too big a number before the second step is shown. Watch for students who stop after multiplying by ten.

source: Roxie evaluated 116 × 5 by multiplying by 10 and halving; Estu evaluated 824 × 25 by multiplying by 100 and dividing by 4
video_script.why: The child multiplies and divides whole numbers, and now uses a place-value shift and a division to make a hard product easy.
video_script.substitution: Replace times 5 by times 10 then divide by 2, and times 25 by times 100 then divide by 4.
video_script.anchor: The two products 116 × 5 and 824 × 25 side by side, with a speech card for each name.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko multiplies 116 by 10, gets 1160 and calls it the answer. That is the answer for times 10; times 5 is half of it, which is 580.
video_script.payoff_line: The two products are five hundred eighty and twenty thousand six hundred

final_answer.spoken: five hundred eighty, and twenty thousand six hundred

never_show: either final product before the answer beat
video_script.design: One idea: times 5 is times 10 then halve; times 25 is times 100 then divide by 4. Wrong idea: Keeko stops after times 10. The anchor stays all video; the working band builds in the idea part; no hard clear.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Ruhee finds one hundred sixteen times five, by multiplying by ten and then halving.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Laksh finds eight hundred twenty four times twenty five. The method is to multiply by one hundred, and then divide by four.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Can we do both the same way?

beats.on_screen: the anchor holds still and gets an accent underline; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: cards: 5 = 10 ÷ 2; 25 = 100 ÷ 4; multiplying by 10 or 100 only adds zeros at the end

marks.m3: the card for adding zeros appears

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Five is ten divided by two.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Twenty five is one hundred divided by four.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Multiplying by ten or one hundred only adds zeros at the end.

marks.m1: the given line is written in the working band

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, one hundred sixteen times five, and eight hundred twenty four times twenty five.

beats.on_screen: To find: both products with the two shortcuts

marks.m1: the find line is written under the given line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find both products with the two shortcuts.

marks.m2: a zero joins the end of 116 to make 1160
marks.m3: a note appears that 1160 is for times 10, not times 5

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, Ruhee multiplies one hundred sixteen by ten, and halves the result.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Ten times one hundred sixteen puts a zero at the end of the digits.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>This number is for times ten, so it is too big for times five.

marks.m3: 500 + 80 is written as the next line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, halve it. Half of one thousand is five hundred.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Half of one hundred sixty is eighty.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>We add the two halves.

marks.m2: two zeros join the end of 824 to make 82,400

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, Laksh multiplies eight hundred twenty four by one hundred, and divides the result by four.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two zeros join the end of the digits.

marks.m3: 20,000 + 600 is written as the next line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, divide by four. Eighty thousand divided by four is twenty thousand.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two thousand four hundred divided by four is six hundred.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>We add the two parts.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>The two products are five hundred eighty and twenty thousand six hundred.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Both came from one shift of zeros and one split.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the board
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: 116 × 5 = 1160 crossed out; 116 × 10 = 1160 and half of it written beside

marks.m3: an arrow marks the halving step

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks one hundred sixteen times five is one thousand one hundred sixty. Keeko multiplied by ten and stopped there.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But that is the answer for times ten, and five is only half of ten.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Keeko forgot the halving step, so the answer must be half of it.
